description: We’re a team of six ELTE  students passionate about technology and innovation. Our interests and skills span AI/ML, software development, cybersecurity, web development, and game development. We enjoy building practical projects, solving challenging problems, and learning new technologies along the way.
summary:
One More Sol is a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer game that puts a 7 to 12 year old in command of a Mars base for ten sols. Each turn the player spends limited solar power on cards: run research, grow food, charge the backup battery, or take shelter. Three meters decide everything: health, power and radiation.

The twist is that the danger is real. On sol 9, the Sun flares and the base is hit by the actual solar storm of September 2017, replayed from NASA DONKI space weather records and published radiation measurements for the Mars surface. Players who saved power for the shelter survive it. Players who did not learn why astronauts hide behind thick walls.

There is no rules page. Pip, a small robot, teaches the game inside the first four turns, so children learn by doing. Space weather is one of the biggest obstacles to sending people to Mars. We turned it into something a child can feel, plan for and beat.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

One More Sol is a browser game for ages 7 to 12. The player commands a Mars base for ten sols (Mars days) and has to keep three meters healthy: health, energy power and radiation. It is live at onemoresol.earth and also runs offline by opening one file.

HOW IT WORKS

Each sol has five turns, four in daylight and one at night. A turn starts with an event: a dust storm that dims the solar panels, a freezing night, broken equipment, a supply box, a message from Earth. The player then picks cards, limited by the power in the battery: run research, grow food, charge the backup battery, take shelter, explore outside, or crank a generator by hand as a last resort. Research adds up to discoveries, and each discovery unlocks an upgrade for the base. Calling Earth for advice costs power and the answer arrives one or two turns later, because radio signals really are that slow.

On sol 9 the Sun flares. The base is then hit by the real solar storm of September 2017, replayed turn by turn from NASA DONKI space weather records and published radiation measurements for the surface of Mars. In the shelter the crew takes a quarter of the dose. Outside, they can pass the safe limit within a few turns. The end screen tells the player the storm really happened and explains the three decisions that mattered most in their game, each paired with a real fact and its source.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Children do not read rules, so there are none. A robot called Pip teaches the whole game inside four real turns, highlighting one thing at a time and waiting until the child has done it. A child who has run out of power during a solar storm understands space weather in a way a paragraph cannot teach. We want players to leave knowing why Mars has no magnetic shield, why sunlight is scarce there, and why astronauts need shelter, and to feel that these are problems they could solve. The game needs no account, no install and no internet, so it works in classrooms and on old school computers and phones.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript, with no framework and no build step. The rules are kept separate from the page, so a Node.js test script plays thousands of simulated missions with different play styles to check the balance. Sounds are generated in the browser with the Web Audio API. Storm data comes from NASA DONKI and from Matthia, Meier and Berger (2018).

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

The villain of the game is a real event with real data behind it, not an invented monster. The start screen is a small physics scene: a robot hovering on thrusters and a landing module touching down in a cloud of dust, both pulled by the same Mars gravity value. The launch is an airlock sequence instead of a loading screen. Every icon is drawn as pixel art in code. A lost mission never ends in tragedy: the crew flies home early and the player is invited to try again.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Reading level: short sentences and one idea at a time. Honesty: a Sources page lists where every number comes from and where the game simplifies reality, for example that the storm is scaled up so it matters in a ten-sol mission. Fairness: careless play loses, careful play can always win. Accessibility: players with reduced motion switched on skip the animations, and sound can be turned off on every screen. Privacy: nothing leaves the player's device.
